Ways to work

As a team

Several people, several machines, one repository. The ledger shows who holds what, and a hand-off puts a blocker in front of the right person.

On this page
  • Does setup turn the ledger on?
  • The ledger
  • Claims and leases
  • The inbox
  • Who owns an area

  • Growth and retention

Most people only need

  • Setup turns the ledger on only if you answer yes (GitHub mode). Otherwise turn it on by hand.
  • Each teammate runs /sigma-ledger once in their own clone to join.
  • A claim is a lease that expires after 12 hours, so a crashed session cannot block the team.
  • Blocked on someone else's area? Hand it off instead of parking it.
  • Everything else on this page is optional and off by default.

When more than one person runs the loop, each loop needs to know what the others are doing, or two people will build the same goal. The ledger is a shared log on its own git branch: who claimed which goal, how it ended, notes, and hand-offs. A hand-off is how a loop says "this is blocked on something in your area" without parking into silence: it opens an issue assigned to the right person.

Does setup turn the ledger on?

Not unless you say yes. The shipped config leaves ledger.enabled undecided (null), and undecided reads as off. What each way of setting up does:

You runResult for ledger.enabled
/sigma-init in GitHub modeAsks one question (an [ask] line). --ledger yes writes true, --ledger no writes false. Unanswered, it stays undecided and the question is asked again on the next run.
/sigma-init --yesTakes the safe default for an open question: false. It changes nothing on a repository whose config already answers it.
/sigma-init in local-files modeNo ledger question. The key stays undecided, so off.
/sigma-setupAn alias that runs the same flow with the same questions, so the same results. It does not turn the ledger on by itself.
Re-running with an answer already in configKept. A value in config is never re-applied over; only a flag on the current run changes it.

Answering yes writes the setting only. The flow then prints the command that creates and pushes the ledger branch and does not run it, because it pushes a branch. To turn it on by hand, put this in .sdlc/config.json, then ask /sigma-ledger to set it up:

"ledger": { "enabled": true }

/sigma-init also creates an empty .sdlc/ledger/ folder holding only a README, whatever you answer. Each teammate runs the setup once in their own clone. /sigma-doctor sets it up if the ledger is enabled but missing.

The ledger

QuestionAnswer
Where it livesA branch named sdlc-ledger, checked out as a worktree at .sdlc/ledger/. Pulling it never touches your working tree. The worktree must stay git-ignored so it never lands in a code pull request, and the branch is never merged into your integration branch, so it needs no review.
Why many filesEach writing process writes only its own entry file, so concurrent writers cannot conflict. The team view is their union, computed on read. Expect hundreds of files per person; that is the healthy state, and exactly one file for an actor means that actor's writes stopped.
Reading it/sigma-ledger shows what is addressed to you, a one-line team summary, and a regenerated TEAM.md rollup. Never edit TEAM.md by hand.
Writing itClaims and outcomes are written for you. You write by hand only for a note or a hand-off. A write you type publishes itself and says on stderr whether the team can see it yet; ledger.publish_on_write: false keeps it local for the watcher to carry.
Your name on itledger.actor, else your authenticated GitHub account, else your shell user. File names carry a short hash of the machine, never the machine name. Two optional keys change it: ledger.host_alias (a label of letters and digits, at most 12) and ledger.salt_host_token (a different token per repository). Changing either re-roots the machine once, so choose once.
Fail-openA ledger problem never stops a run.

Claims and leases

RuleDetail
A pick skips what is heldWith the ledger on, a pick skips any goal another actor, or another live process of your own, already holds.
A claim is a leaseIt expires ledger.lease.ttl_hours after the claim (default 12) unless renewed.
RenewalA run that holds a claim writes a renewal at goal boundaries, at most once per a third of the TTL. Only a renewal by the holder (same actor, same machine, compatible run) extends it, and one dated more than 15 minutes ahead of the reader's clock is ignored.
Reclaiming a stale claimA claim written on this machine is released when expired. A claim written on another machine is released only after a fresh read-only fetch of the ledger branch still shows it open and expired. A failed fetch releases nothing and says why.
A session that dies without startingGoals it claimed but never started are released on the next pick, after session_release.grace_minutes (default 15). A live session that sits on a claimed, unstarted goal longer than session_release.hold_minutes (default 30; 0 turns it off) has it released too. A started goal is never released.
Advisory, not a lockA lease sees only claims already synced to the ledger branch.

The inbox

Anything addressed to you (a hand-off, a note, a new comment on a goal you hold) is written to .sdlc/state/inbox.md by the watcher. The loop prints that inbox on stderr before it hands over the next goal. That boundary is deliberate: nothing can inject a message into a running session, and interrupting a goal mid-flight loses work. The worst-case delay is one goal, so a top-priority item is taken next, not now. Two suppressions keep it quiet: a per-author cursor so history is not re-read, and a signature on the kind, issue and state so a colleague's rebase cannot replay old mentions. A change of state on the same issue does fire.

Who owns an area

A hand-off is addressed to the owner of an area. Sigma looks the name up in this order, and the first match wins.

OrderSourceUse it for
1ledger.owners in .sdlc/config.json: a map from area to loginAn area name that is not a directory. For example web-ui is the label for work inside frontend/, which the lookup cannot guess.
2.github/CODEOWNERS (also CODEOWNERS or docs/CODEOWNERS); the area is tried as a directoryEverything it can resolve on its own. Leave those areas out of the map so there is one roster to change.
3The * catch-all, only if nothing more specific matchedA repository with one owner needs nothing else.

The roster is advisory, on purpose. CODEOWNERS auto-assigns reviewers but no branch rule requires their approval, because a binding rule with several owners lets each block the other, and Sigma's own merge handler can stall on a pull request it opened. To make it binding, enable Require review from Code Owners on the branch and grant Sigma's account a bypass first, or every automated merge waits on a person. Unit ownership (who owns a unit of work) is a different thing; see Units of work.

Assignment and hand-offs

  • The shipped config has no assignee filter; /sigma-init in GitHub mode sets discovery.github.assignee to @me where it is unset. With that set, the loop works only issues assigned to the person running it. Reassign by editing the issue.
  • When a goal is blocked on someone else's area, ask /sigma-ledger to hand it off instead of parking. It finds the owner (above), opens an issue in their area assigned to them and carrying the goal label, records a hand-off addressed to them, and links it from the blocked issue. Their own loop picks it up through the assignee filter.
  • They answer with one of accepted, deferred, declined or resolved. deferred does not settle it; the hand-off stays outstanding until resolved or declined. A goal blocked on two areas is two independent hand-offs.
  • Every step degrades honestly: with no owner found, no gh, or a local backlog, the ledger entry is still written.
  • Not every finding is a block. A same-area follow-up found mid-goal is filed through the same machinery without parking anything. On an autonomous run it is queued at a low priority for triage rather than made immediately pickable.

Optional watchers

The loop starts a background watcher when you run it; it pulls and publishes the ledger every ledger.watch.interval_seconds (default 900) and refreshes the inbox. Stop it with touch .sdlc/state/watch.stop. The three below are separate switches on top of it.

SettingDoesNeeds
agent_watch.enabledNotifies when a claimed goal's registered process is confirmed dead: an email if agent_watch.notify.email is configured, always a ledger note otherwise. Exactly once per dead process.ledger on
comment_watch.enabledNotifies the claimant of a new comment on a claimed issue, as a ledger note. Your own comments are suppressed.ledger on, GitHub source
ledger.autowatch.enabledWhen a new item addressed to you arrives, drives the loop on that one flagged issue, never an open-ended pick, after its preconditions pass (a logged-in gh, no concurrent session, an optional load ceiling, an optional weekly spend ceiling). hop_limit caps chained runs.ledger on

All three are off by default. Each is opt-in and none starts without you turning it on. Email never accepts a literal password: pass_env names an environment variable, and SMTP settings that come from the repository are refused unless you export SIGMA_ALLOW_REPO_SMTP=1 in your own shell. A failed send falls back to a ledger note. The autowatch webhook accepts only loopback hosts unless you set allow_remote_webhook.

Growth and retention

ItemBehaviour
Ledger entry filesNever compacted and never pruned. Every run adds a file. Nothing is read back by file name, so the count costs correctness nothing; read cost grows with use.
Local action logA separate, local, git-ignored trace, not the ledger. It is pruned: action_log.retention_days defaults to 90 with a floor of 30.
Dependency-map historyWith the ledger on and the dependency map not off, it is mirrored to the ledger branch and rolled up in a DAG.md that lists ticket numbers only.

Limits

LimitWhat it means
Two picks at the same instantCovered only on one machine, by a POSIX file lock. Across machines, a lease sees only claims already synced.
WindowsThat lock is unavailable. The ledger's publish commands refuse and defer unless you set SIGMA_LEDGER_ALLOW_UNSERIALISED to 1, accepting that two publishers in one checkout can then collide.
A diverged ledgerA clone whose ledger branch shares no history with the remote's (a branch deleted and recreated, say) cannot publish. /sigma-doctor shows DIVERGED. Re-running the setup re-roots it onto the remote's branch, keeps your own entry files and saves the old tip under a recovery ref. It never runs on its own.
Mixed versionsAn older Sigma ignores lease renewals and per-area answers, so upgrade every machine before relying on either.
Single-branch or shallow clonesWork with no extra step: every ledger fetch names the branch.
